paras: The lynching of Sam and John Campbell took place about midnight on December 23, 1880, when a crowd of seventy-five to one hundred men took the two Black brothers from the jail at Munfordville, Hart County, Kentucky, and hanged them from a tree below the town. The brothers had been arrested that day on suspicion of beating and robbing John A. Gardner, a magistrate described as one of the county's most prominent citizens. Wire dispatches carried the story to papers across the country within two days, and digests of it were still being printed in mid-January 1881.

According to a Horse Cave special to the Louisville Courier-Journal, Sam Campbell lived with Gardner about a mile from Rowlett's Station, and his brother John, who lived in the neighborhood, had stayed the night at Gardner's. The same account said the brothers "had only been in the country a few months."

About five o'clock on the morning of Thursday, December 23, a Campbell called Gardner to his stable, saying one of his cows was sick. On entering, Gardner was struck on the head and face with a stick of wood and robbed of about $130. The shorter Horse Cave wire said Campbell then told Mrs. Gardner what had happened and helped carry her husband into the house. Suspicion nonetheless fell on the two brothers, who were arrested and searched; money, and in the Courier-Journal's version a pocketbook that Mrs. Gardner identified, was reported found on them.

The brothers were committed to the jail at Munfordville, where about midnight a party of men demanded the keys. The Courier-Journal special said the jailer, seeing it "would be useless to resist," handed over the keys after asking that the other prisoners be left alone, while a Louisville wire said masked men overpowered him. The men led the prisoners through the streets and down a hillside between the town and the river, where both were hanged from the limb of a tree. It was said that Sam, the younger, confessed before he died and blamed John, who would say only that his people lived in Taylor County.

A coroner's jury of six held an inquest and, in the Courier-Journal's words, "returned a verdict in accordance with the facts." Gardner was reported in critical condition with several wounds to his face and head, and no later report of his death or recovery was found. No arrest of any member of the mob appears in the coverage.

Three separate dispatches reached the national press on Christmas Day: the Horse Cave wire, a briefer Louisville wire, and a Cincinnati Star special from Munfordville. The Chicago Tribune printed the fuller Courier-Journal special under the heading "Two Murderous and Thieving Negroes Lynched by a Kentucky Mob," and the Rock Island Argus reprinted it with the opening line "Side by side they hang on the banks of Green river." Headlines varied in tone, from "Swift Retribution for Murderers" in New Haven and "Negro Robbers Hanged by a Mob" in Dallas to "Kentucky Lawlessness" in Washington.

Several Northern papers treated the lynching as characteristic of the state, with the Wheeling Intelligencer calling it "The Usual Kentucky Tragedy" and the Indiana State Sentinel heading it "How They Serve 'Em in Kentucky." None of these papers questioned the accusation, and the Sentinel's weekly summary said the two had been lynched "for an assault on and robbery of a white man." Weekly digests from Minnesota to Mississippi reduced the story to a sentence, some calling the lynchers "one hundred citizens of Munfordville" and some later versions claiming that both brothers had confessed.

Accounts differ on the size of the crowd, given as seventy-five by a Louisville wire, "seventy-five or one hundred" by the Courier-Journal special, and one hundred by the Horse Cave wire. The detailed account attributes a confession only to Sam and only as hearsay, while later digests said both brothers confessed after their arrest. Some briefs placed the jail or the lynching at "Roulletteville" or "Romletts" station or near Horse Cave, but the fuller Kentucky accounts put the jail and the hanging at Munfordville and the robbery near Rowlett's Station.

Sam and John Campbell were hanged by a party of seventy-five to one hundred men who took them from jail without lawful authority, in retribution for the robbery and beating of J. A. Gardner of which they were accused (A8, A2, A6).

At least four separately sourced reports, the Courier-Journal's Horse Cave special (A8, A15), the Horse Cave wire (A2, A6, A14), a Louisville wire (A1, A3) and a Cincinnati Star special (A7), agree that a mob took the two Campbell brothers from jail and hanged them.

framing.detail: The New Haven Morning Journal and Courier headed the wire 'Swift Retribution for Murderers', though Gardner was alive.
The Chicago Tribune ran the Courier-Journal special under 'Two Murderous and Thieving Negroes Lynched by a Kentucky Mob', presenting the accusation as fact.
Northern headlines 'The Usual Kentucky Tragedy', 'How They Serve 'Em in Kentucky' and 'Kentucky Lawlessness' cast the lynching as typical of the state while printing the accusation unchallenged.
Most papers, including the Sun, Richmond Dispatch and Dallas Herald, printed the Horse Cave wire under plain headlines such as 'Lynch Law in Kentucky' and 'Negro Robbers Hanged by a Mob'.

Sam Campbell (the younger, about 20) and his brother John Campbell (about 22 or 23), described as 'negroes'.
